### Highest-Leverage Change: Add the Five Missing Slides

This is not five separate fixes — it is one structural gap that accounts for the majority of your 18 failures. The deck is currently 6 slides. A seed-stage deck needs 10-12. The missing slides are: **Why Now, Market Sizing, Competition, Business Model, and GTM.** Every one of these is a critical omission at seed.

Here's why each one matters from an investor's seat:

- **Why Now** answers the question every investor is silently asking: "If this problem has existed for years, why will it get solved in the next 18 months?" Per Sequoia's "Why wasn't this built before?" standard, the absence of a why-now slide signals either that you haven't thought about market timing or that the timing isn't actually compelling. Either reading is damaging.

- **Market Sizing** done bottom-up (ICP count × willingness to pay × adoption rate) shows you understand your customers. A top-down TAM number ("$50B market") tells investors nothing — they've seen it a thousand times. A bottom-up calculation shows discipline. This is a non-negotiable for seed per standard VC practice.

- **Competition** is the slide most founders dread and most investors scrutinize hardest. DocSend data shows investors spend 88% more time on competition in funded decks versus unfunded ones. An absent competition slide doesn't signal you have no competitors — it signals you haven't done the work, or you're hiding something. Neither is acceptable. Show the landscape honestly. Your differentiation will be more credible for it.

- **Business Model** needs to answer three questions: Who pays? How much? What are the margins? Without this, "raising $1.2M seed" floats in a vacuum — investors can't model what the business looks like at scale, and they won't ask in a meeting what they couldn't figure out from the deck.

- **GTM** (go-to-market) should show your ICP, the channel, and early proof of that channel working. Developer tools live or die on distribution. Ex-Stripe and ex-Notion should have strong intuitions here — surface them.

Adding these five slides with real content will raise your score substantially and, more importantly, will make the deck fundable.

### The AI Claim Needs Resolution

Your deck uses "AI-native" in the tagline but contains no AI-specific content anywhere. This is your most credibility-damaging issue and it compounds every other weakness.

Investors reading a seed deck in 2026 are acutely attuned to unsubstantiated AI claims. > Pre-Seed, Seed, and Series A
## What "effective" means in 2026

A pitch deck is not a brochure or a business plan. It is a **fast filter that earns the next conversation**—a meeting, then diligence. Three realities shape what "good" looks like:

1. **Attention is brutally compressed.** Investors spend **\~2:30 of real attention** on a share deck (DocSend/Dropbox 2024 data; earlier 3:44 figure is from 2015 and should not be used as a 2026 baseline). Early-stage decks may get even less. 31% of readers bounce within the first 10 seconds; 78% abandon before slide 6. But if a reader reaches slide 4, 82% will finish. Design accordingly.
2. **Capital efficiency is back in the underwriting.** Investors expect founders to know burn, runway, and efficiency metrics (e.g., burn multiple) and to tie dollars to milestones. Growth-at-all-costs is dead.
3. **The bar for "Series A readiness" keeps rising.** Carta Q2 2025 data shows the new Series A bar is ~$3M ARR (some VCs expect $5M–$10M); the median seed-to-A timeline has stretched to ~20 months, with 25% of companies taking 3.5+ years. Only ~18–20% of seed-funded companies graduate to Series A.

---

## Non-negotiable principles (every stage)

### 1. Start with a one-sentence company purpose

Sequoia explicitly recommends defining the company in a single declarative sentence. This is the anchor for everything else.

**Formats that work:**
- "[Category] for [ICP] that delivers [quantified outcome]."
- "We replace [expensive/manual process] with [new workflow], cutting [time/cost] by [X]."
- "The system of record for [job-to-be-done] in [vertical]."

**Rule:** If a smart investor can't repeat what you do after 10 seconds, your deck is failing.

### 2. Slide headlines must carry the story

Investors skim headlines first. Each headline should be a **conclusion, not a topic**: "Retention is 92% at 6 months" beats "Retention."

### 3. The narrative flow must feel inevitable

The core arc—**Problem → Solution → Why now → Proof → Ask**—is consistent across Sequoia, DocSend, and YC frameworks. Every source agrees: tell a story, don't present a data dump.

### 4. Never dodge competition

- DocSend data: VCs spent **88% more time** on the competition section in successful decks vs. unsuccessful ones.
- "No competition" reads as naivety, not differentiation. Map direct competitors + incumbents + "do nothing" / internal build.
- Use 2–3 concrete differentiators (speed, cost, distribution, data advantage, regulatory fit, switching costs).

### 5. Prove you're building, not just proposing

Even at pre-seed, show a prototype, alpha/beta, design partners, or real-world usage. The era of "Minimum Viable PowerPoint" is over (DocSend).

### 6. Treat the deck as the front door to diligence

Your deck must be consistent with what you'll show in the data room (numbers, claims, logos, timelines). a16z's data room guide: at minimum, have cap table + historical P&L + burn ready.

---

## Deck formats to build

| Format | Purpose | Slides | Key requirement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Share deck** (emailed) | Gets meetings. Optimized for skimming, forwardable internally. | 10–12 core + appendix | Every slide must stand alone without your narration |
| **Live deck** (presented) | Supports your verbal pitch. Fewer words, more visuals. | 8–12 | Amplifies the spoken word; never distracts from it |
| **Data deck** (separate file) | Answers deep questions (cohorts, funnels, unit economics, pipeline, architecture, security). | Variable | Keep separate—don't stuff extra slides into the main deck |

Storydoc data: ~10-slide decks achieve the highest completion rate (32% vs. 22% average), with sharp engagement drop-off after ~18 slides.

---

## The baseline slide framework

Based on Sequoia's "Writing a Business Plan" + modern additions from DocSend, YC, a16z, and Carta data:

### Slide 1 — Company purpose + "what you sell"
- One sentence + one proof point: traction metric, customer count, pilot, or "built by ex-X team."

### Slide 2 — Problem (pain, owner, cost of inaction)
- Identify the user/buyer and the moment of pain.
- Quantify: time, money, risk, regulatory exposure, missed revenue.
- Use concrete examples or customer quotes—not industry-level abstractions.

### Slide 3 — Solution (workflow change, not feature list)
- Show the "before → after."
- Product screenshot or 3-step flow when possible.
- Focus on value delivered, not technical architecture.

### Slide 4 — Why now (macro shift + wedge timing)
- Sequoia: "Why wasn't this built before?"
- Strongest at pre-seed/seed. By Series A, traction should speak for itself.
- Catalysts: regulatory shift, new platform primitive, behavioral change, cost curve collapse.

### Slide 5 — Market potential (TAM with credibility)
- **Bottom-up sizing beats generic TAM charts.** Show: ICP count x willingness to pay x adoption rate assumptions.
- Expandability (adjacent segments) as a second layer.
- Avoid inflated billion-dollar claims without justification.

### Slide 6 — Traction / proof (stage-dependent)
- Move this earlier if traction is strong (the "Slide 4 Rule": 82% finish if hooked by slide 4).
- Stage-appropriate metrics (see stage-specific sections below).

### Slide 7 — Competition / alternatives (and why you win)
- Map direct competitors + incumbents + "do nothing."
- 2–3 concrete differentiators. Avoid generic 2x2 matrices without explanation.

### Slide 8 — Business model (how money flows)
- Pricing model (seat, usage, outcome, per workflow, take-rate).
- Who pays (buyer) vs. who uses (user).
- Gross margin structure (especially important for AI/compute-heavy products).

## Coaching Commentary

### What's Working — Protect These

**1. The problem is quantified.** "20+ hours/week" is a real number. Most early-stage decks say "developers are frustrated" and stop there. You've put a time cost on the pain, which is the first move toward making it feel urgent. Per YC's "problem before solution" principle, quantified pain dramatically increases investor engagement.

**2. The founding team has legitimate pedigree.** Ex-Stripe (eng) and ex-Notion (product) is a credible pairing for a developer-tooling company. Stripe is one of the most respected engineering cultures in the industry; Notion brings product-led growth intuition. That combination signals you understand both the technical infrastructure and the adoption dynamics. Investors will notice.

**3. The core narrative spine exists.** Problem → Solution → Team → Ask is the fundamental arc, and you have it. Many decks at this stage are a disconnected collection of slides. You have a thread. That's a foundation to build on, not start over from.

### Highest-Leverage Change: Add the Five Missing Slides

This is not five separate fixes — it is one structural gap that accounts for the majority of your 18 failures. The deck is currently 6 slides. A seed-stage deck needs 10-12. The missing slides are: **Why Now, Market Sizing, Competition, Business Model, and GTM.** Every one of these is a critical omission at seed.

Here's why each one matters from an investor's seat:

- **Why Now** answers the question every investor is silently asking: "If this problem has existed for years, why will it get solved in the next 18 months?" Per Sequoia's "Why wasn't this built before?" standard, the absence of a why-now slide signals either that you haven't thought about market timing or that the timing isn't actually compelling. Either reading is damaging.

- **Market Sizing** done bottom-up (ICP count × willingness to pay × adoption rate) shows you understand your customers. A top-down TAM number ("$50B market") tells investors nothing — they've seen it a thousand times. A bottom-up calculation shows discipline. This is a non-negotiable for seed per standard VC practice.

- **Competition** is the slide most founders dread and most investors scrutinize hardest. DocSend data shows investors spend 88% more time on competition in funded decks versus unfunded ones. An absent competition slide doesn't signal you have no competitors — it signals you haven't done the work, or you're hiding something. Neither is acceptable. Show the landscape honestly. Your differentiation will be more credible for it.

- **Business Model** needs to answer three questions: Who pays? How much? What are the margins? Without this, "raising $1.2M seed" floats in a vacuum — investors can't model what the business looks like at scale, and they won't ask in a meeting what they couldn't figure out from the deck.

- **GTM** (go-to-market) should show your ICP, the channel, and early proof of that channel working. Developer tools live or die on distribution. Ex-Stripe and ex-Notion should have strong intuitions here — surface them.

Adding these five slides with real content will raise your score substantially and, more importantly, will make the deck fundable.

Your deck uses "AI-native" in the tagline but contains no AI-specific content anywhere. This is your most credibility-damaging issue and it compounds every other weakness.

Investors reading a seed deck in 2026 are acutely attuned to unsubstantiated AI claims. "AI-native" without any of the following — ML in the value prop, inference costs in COGS, foundation model or fine-tuning mention, AI-specific retention metrics — reads as either marketing inflation or confusion about what the product actually does. Per a16z's AI company evaluation framework, an API wrapper without a moat is not defensible, and a claim without proof is worse than no claim at all.

You have two paths: (1) Remove "AI-native" from the positioning until you can substantiate it with specific AI capabilities, compute economics, and defensibility narrative. (2) Add a slide that shows what the AI actually does, what data flywheel or workflow embeddedness creates lock-in, and what your path to 60%+ gross margins looks like as inference costs are real COGS. Path 2 is the right long-term answer. Path 1 is the right move for this fundraise if the AI capabilities aren't production-ready yet.

---

### The Ask Slide Needs Three More Sentences

Slide 6 has the right number ($1.2M seed at $8M post) but stops there. The 2026 fundraising standard requires tying dollars to milestones to next-round readiness. Investors want to know: what does $1.2M buy you, what does "success" look like in 18 months, and what metrics will you need to raise your Series A? Three sentences. Add them.

---

### Would an Investor Take the Meeting?

At 21.2% (major revision), the honest answer is: not from a cold read. The deck as it stands signals a very early-stage product with incomplete investor preparation — not necessarily a bad company, but a deck that hasn't finished communicating the opportunity.

The path to a meeting is not polish — it's completing the story. Your team is credible, the problem is real, and the core arc exists. Fill in the five missing slides with honest, specific content, resolve the AI positioning, and tie the ask to milestones. That deck — even without perfect design — is one that warrants a 30-minute call. The current version raises more questions than it answers, and investors won't ask questions they expect the deck to have covered.

## Slide-by-Slide Feedback

*Each slide assessment is the agent's evaluation against best-practice frameworks. Strengths and weaknesses are the agent's analysis, not investor quotes.*

### Slide 1: "Acmecorp — AI-native developer tools for indie SaaS founders" (Company purpose / Title)

**What's working:**
- The tagline 'AI-native developer tools for indie SaaS founders' establishes a clear ICP (indie SaaS founders) and a product category in a single line.
- The company name is memorable and the slide establishes a niche positioning that differentiates from broad developer-tools platforms.
**What investors will question:**
- The purpose statement is a tagline, not a declarative outcome sentence. It names the category but does not quantify the value delivered — investors cannot immediately grasp what 'AI-native' means in practice or what outcome the ICP achieves.
- No proof point on the title slide. Sequoia and DocSend both recommend a traction metric, customer count, or credibility signal on the opening slide to hook the reader immediately.
- The 'AI-native' claim is unverified: no evidence of AI core value prop, inference costs, or model usage is established on this slide or anywhere in the deck.
  *Principles: Sequoia 'Writing a Business Plan' — define the company in a single declarative sentence with a quantified outcome, DocSend 2024 — 31% of readers bounce within first 10 seconds; opening slide must hook immediately, a16z — AI claims without evidence reduce credibility in an AI-saturated market*

**How to fix:**
- Rewrite to a declarative outcome sentence following Sequoia's format: '[Category] for [ICP] that delivers [quantified outcome].' For example: 'Acmecorp eliminates 20+ hours/week of tooling integration for indie SaaS founders — one CLI connecting GitHub, Linear, Stripe, and Vercel.'
- Add a traction proof point on the title slide (e.g., '$8K MRR, 24 paying customers, 18% MoM growth') so the first impression signals momentum, per DocSend's guidance that 31% of readers bounce within 10 seconds.
- Either substantiate the 'AI-native' claim with a concrete capability statement on this slide, or remove it to avoid triggering skepticism without follow-through — per a16z's warning that 'AI-first' claims without evidence are a credibility risk in 2026's saturated market.

### Slide 2: "Indie SaaS founders waste 20+ hours/week on developer tooling integration" (Problem)

**What's working:**
- The problem quantifies time lost: '20+ hours/week on developer tooling integration' is concrete and memorable.
- The ICP is specific: indie SaaS founders — a well-defined buyer/user segment.
**What investors will question:**
- The quantification is a single time-cost metric with no source cited. Investors will ask: where does '20+ hours/week' come from? Customer discovery calls? Survey data? Without sourcing, it reads as an estimate.
- No cost-of-inaction framing: there is no dollar cost, risk, or urgency signal tied to the 20+ hours. Sequoia's framework requires identifying the budget owner and the cost of inaction, not just the time lost.
- No customer quote, concrete example, or 'moment of pain' narrative. The slide states the problem at an industry-level abstraction rather than making it visceral.
- No urgency signal: why is this problem being solved now versus two years ago? The deck lacks a 'why now' slide entirely, so the problem slide carries extra burden to establish timeliness.
  *Principles: Sequoia framework — identify user/buyer, moment of pain, and quantify cost of inaction with concrete examples or customer quotes, Common mistakes guidance — 'nice to have' problem without urgency, budget owner, and cost of inaction kills momentum, DocSend — use concrete examples or customer quotes, not industry-level abstractions*

**How to fix:**
- Source the '20+ hours/week' claim — even 'from interviews with 30 indie SaaS founders' adds credibility, per Sequoia's guidance on using concrete evidence or customer quotes.
- Add a cost-of-inaction frame: translate 20 hours/week into lost revenue, delayed product cycles, or competitive disadvantage. For example: 'At a $200K founder salary, that's $50K/year in lost productivity per founder.'
- Add one concrete customer example or quote illustrating the pain moment — e.g., 'Every time I ship a new feature I spend 3 days rewiring Stripe webhooks and Vercel deploys before I can even test.' This grounds the abstraction, per DocSend best practices.
- Consider adding a 'Why now' catalyst: API ecosystem fragmentation, growth of solo-founder SaaS, or the rise of AI-native CLIs are all credible catalysts that Sequoia explicitly recommends surfacing.

### Slide 3: "Acmecorp wraps GitHub, Linear, Stripe, and Vercel into one CLI" (Solution)

**What's working:**
- The solution is concrete and specific: 'wraps GitHub, Linear, Stripe, and Vercel into one CLI' — investors immediately understand the product's scope.
- Naming four specific integrations (GitHub, Linear, Stripe, Vercel) shows product specificity and resonates with the ICP's known tooling stack.
**What investors will question:**
- The slide is a feature description, not a before→after workflow. Sequoia explicitly requires showing the workflow change — what does the founder's day look like before versus after Acmecorp? The current framing answers 'what it is' but not 'what it does for you.'
- No product screenshot, demo link, or 3-step flow. In 2026, DocSend data makes clear that 'Minimum Viable PowerPoint' is no longer accepted at seed stage — product evidence is required.
- The 'AI-native' positioning from the title slide is not substantiated here. There is no explanation of what AI does in the CLI, creating a disconnect between the brand claim and the product description.
- No value quantification: how much time does Acmecorp save compared to the 20+ hours cited in the problem? The solution slide should close the loop on the problem metric.
  *Principles: Sequoia, DocSend — solution must show 'before → after' workflow change, not a feature list, DocSend — 'Minimum Viable PowerPoint' era is over; product screenshot or 3-step flow required at seed, Common mistakes — 'features instead of outcomes' is one of the most reliably fatal deck patterns*

**How to fix:**
- Restructure around a 'before → after' workflow: 'Before: 6 manual steps across 4 tools to deploy a feature. After: one CLI command.' This follows Sequoia's and DocSend's core guidance on solution framing.
- Add a product screenshot, CLI demo output, or 3-step visual flow. Even a text-based CLI example counts as product evidence and significantly increases credibility at seed stage.
- Explicitly connect to the AI claim: describe what the AI layer does (e.g., intelligent routing, automated conflict resolution, natural language commands) so 'AI-native' becomes a feature benefit, not a buzzword.
- Close the loop on the problem: quantify the time saved (e.g., 'reduces 20+ hours/week to under 2') to create a tight problem-solution narrative, per Sequoia's framework.

### Slide 4: "$8K MRR, 24 paying customers, 18% MoM growth (last 4 months)" (Traction)

**What's working:**
- Three concrete metrics are cited verbatim: '$8K MRR, 24 paying customers, 18% MoM growth (last 4 months)' — this is the right format for a seed traction slide.
- '18% MoM growth (last 4 months)' is a strong signal: if sustained, it implies ~2.2x growth in 4 months and approaches the 'triple triple double double' growth pattern investors watch for.
- The combination of MRR, customer count, and growth rate covers three of the five key B2B SaaS traction metrics for seed stage.
**What investors will question:**
- $8K MRR is early for a seed round. Carta and SaaStr data indicate seed investors increasingly expect $300K–$500K ARR signals ($25K–$42K MRR equivalent) for B2B SaaS. $8K MRR annualizes to ~$96K ARR — well below that threshold.
- No retention or churn data. The seed-stage traction framework requires churn/retention as a key metric alongside MRR and growth. Growth without retention evidence is a red flag cited explicitly in the seed-stage best practices.
- No NRR, expansion revenue, or average contract value (ACV) shown. With 24 customers, the average MRR per customer is ~$333/month — useful context that is absent.
- No CAC or payback period data. Seed-stage investors expect early channel proof and unit economics signals.
- 'Last 4 months' is a short window. Investors will want to know if this growth is accelerating, steady, or decelerating — a growth chart would show the trend more credibly than a single average.
  *Principles: Seed-stage traction framework — B2B SaaS: ARR/MRR, MoM growth, churn/retention, NRR, pipeline, CAC payback all required, Carta/SaaStr 2025 — seed investors increasingly expect $300K–$500K ARR signals for B2B SaaS, Seed red flags — 'growth without retention' is explicitly called out as a seed-stage warning signal, DocSend — use charts over text for traction; growth line beats a single metric*

**How to fix:**
- Add retention data immediately — even a simple '90% MoM retention' or 'zero churn in 4 months' would address the most significant gap. Per seed-stage best practices, growth without retention evidence is a seed red flag.
- Add a growth chart (MRR by month) rather than a single average growth rate. A visual trend is more credible and engaging than a single metric, per DocSend's guidance that charts outperform text for traction.
- State ACV or average MRR per customer to give investors a sense of pricing and expansion potential ($8K MRR / 24 customers = ~$333/month average — worth showing explicitly).
- Acknowledge the early stage honestly and reframe around velocity: 'From $0 to $8K MRR in 4 months, growing 18% MoM with 24 paying customers' positions the trajectory rather than the absolute level.
- Consider moving the traction slide to position 3 or 4 in the deck (before or alongside the solution), per DocSend's 'Slide 4 Rule': if readers reach slide 4, 82% will finish.

### Slide 5: "Two founders, ex-Stripe (eng) and ex-Notion (product)" (Team)

**What's working:**
- Both founders have name-brand pedigrees: 'ex-Stripe (eng) and ex-Notion (product)' — Stripe and Notion are highly regarded in the developer-tools and SaaS ecosystem, directly relevant to the ICP.
- The complementary split (engineering + product) is the right founding team structure for a developer-tools company.
**What investors will question:**
- No names, photos, or LinkedIn links. DocSend data shows the team slide receives ~46 seconds out of ~2:30 total attention (~30% of all reading time). Investors need to be able to verify credentials and get a sense of the founders as people — anonymous 'two founders' is insufficient.
- No founder-market fit narrative. Being ex-Stripe and ex-Notion establishes pedigree but not personal connection to the problem. Did one of the founders experience the 20+ hours/week pain themselves as an indie SaaS founder? That story is missing.
- No advisory board, angels, or notable early investors mentioned, which could add credibility at this stage.
- No team size context: is it still just two founders, or are there early hires? Investors want to understand current team composition.
- No equity or vesting information, though this is typically handled in diligence rather than the deck itself.
  *Principles: DocSend — team slide gets ~46 seconds out of ~2:30 total attention (~30%); invest heavily here, Sequoia, YC — founder-market fit is the most scrutinized element at pre-seed and seed; why are you the right team?, Pre-send checklist — bios, photos, LinkedIn are baseline requirements*

**How to fix:**
- Add full names, professional photos, and LinkedIn URLs. This is a baseline requirement — per DocSend, the team slide gets the most sustained attention of any slide, and anonymous credentials undercut the credibility you're trying to establish.
- Add a founder-market fit story: did one of the founders spend years as an indie SaaS founder before going to Stripe? That narrative directly addresses 'why are you the right team to solve this?' — the most important question at seed stage per all major frameworks.
- Include any notable angels, advisors, or early backers who add domain credibility in developer tools or SaaS infrastructure.
- State current team size and key open roles if relevant to the ask.

### Slide 6: "Raising $1.2M seed at $8M post" (Ask / Use of funds)

**What's working:**
- The raise amount and valuation are stated explicitly: 'Raising $1.2M seed at $8M post' — clarity on terms is a positive signal.
- $1.2M is within the pre-seed/low-seed range, which is appropriate given the early traction ($8K MRR).
**What investors will question:**
- The ask is just a number and valuation — no use of funds, no milestones, no runway calculation. The 2026 standard explicitly requires tying dollars → milestones → next round readiness (or default-alive path).
- $1.2M at $8M post is technically at the low end of seed-stage ranges (Carta 2025 median seed is ~$3.8M), but the valuation is high relative to the current traction ($8K MRR = ~$96K ARR). At 80x ARR, this will face significant investor scrutiny.
- No use-of-funds breakdown: what does $1.2M buy? Headcount? Product development? Customer acquisition? Without this, investors cannot evaluate whether the capital will achieve meaningful milestones.
- No milestone plan: what does the company look like in 18–24 months post-raise? What ARR/MRR or customer milestone triggers the next raise?
- No runway projection: at current burn, how long does $1.2M last? Carta recommends planning 18–24 months minimum.
  *Principles: 2026 standard — tie dollars → milestones → next round readiness (or default-alive path) — this is non-negotiable, a16z 'The 16 Commandments' — explicit fundraising ask + use of funds is required, Carta 2025 — plan 18–24 months of runway minimum; seed-to-A now stretches to 3+ years for many companies, PitchBook/NVCA + Carta 2025 — seed median is ~$3.8M; $1.2M positions this as early seed or pre-seed, which may affect investor categorization*

**How to fix:**
- Add a use-of-funds breakdown (even a simple 3-bucket allocation: e.g., 60% product/eng, 25% GTM, 15% ops) — this is a minimum requirement per a16z and Sequoia.
- Add a milestone plan: 'With $1.2M, we will reach $X MRR by [date], [Y] customers, and [Z] milestone that positions us for a $3M–$5M seed extension or Series A.' Per 2026 standard, every ask must tie dollars to milestones to next financing.
- Address runway explicitly: state how many months of runway $1.2M provides at current and projected burn rates. Carta recommends 18–24 months minimum.
- Either justify the valuation multiple relative to growth trajectory, or consider whether the round size and valuation are calibrated to current traction — $8K MRR at $8M post is an aggressive multiple that will require a strong growth narrative to support.

### Slides to Add

Investors at your stage will expect these:

- **[IMPORTANT]** Why Now: Add a 'Why Now' slide that identifies the macro catalyst making this the right moment to build Acmecorp. Sequoia explicitly asks 'Why wasn't this built before?' Strong candidates: explosion of indie SaaS builders post-AI coding tools (Cursor, Copilot), fragmentation of the modern SaaS stack (40+ tools for a single product), or cost curves on CLI tooling collapsing with LLM APIs. This is especially important at seed stage where traction is early and the timing story carries significant weight.
- **[CRITICAL]** Market Sizing: Add a market sizing slide using bottom-up methodology: estimate the number of indie SaaS founders globally, multiply by willingness to pay (based on current pricing implied by $8K MRR / 24 customers = ~$333/month), and show the serviceable addressable market. A second layer showing expansion to small dev teams or agencies broadens the story. Sequoia and all major frameworks consider bottom-up market sizing non-negotiable — it signals market awareness and validates that the opportunity justifies VC investment.
- **[CRITICAL]** Competition / Alternatives: Add a competition slide mapping direct competitors (e.g., Zapier, Make, custom scripts, individual CLI tools per service), incumbents (GitHub Actions, Vercel CLI, Stripe CLI), and the 'do nothing / build in-house' alternative. Use 2–3 concrete differentiators (speed, unified interface, AI-native orchestration, indie-founder-specific pricing). DocSend data shows VCs spend 88% more time on the competition section in successful decks vs. unsuccessful ones — omitting this slide is one of the most reliably damaging decisions a founder can make.
- **[CRITICAL]** Business Model: Add a business model slide explaining pricing (per seat? per integration? usage-based?), who pays vs. who uses, and the gross margin structure. For an AI-native CLI, investors will specifically want to understand compute/inference costs and the path to healthy gross margins. Per seed-stage best practices, pricing that matches value capture and a clear buyer-vs-user distinction are required — especially for AI/compute-heavy products where gross margin trajectory is a key diligence question.
- **[IMPORTANT]** Go-to-Market: Add a GTM slide defining the ICP acquisition channel (product-led growth via open-source/freemium CLI? developer community? direct outbound?), initial conversion proof (how did the 24 paying customers find Acmecorp?), and the motion for scaling from 24 to 240 customers. Per Sequoia and DocSend frameworks, a GTM slide with ICP, channel, and early conversion proof is required at seed stage.
- **[IMPORTANT]** Financials / Operating Model: Add a simple financial slide showing current burn, gross margin, and an 18–24 month operating model post-raise. At minimum: revenue projection (based on current growth rate), headcount plan, burn rate, and runway calculation. Per a16z and Carta's seed-stage financial standards, a simple operating model with revenue assumptions, gross margin, and runway is required — and showing you track burn multiple and efficiency signals 'operator,' not just 'storyteller.'

### Overall Narrative

The Acmecorp deck has a strong core: a specific ICP, a quantified problem, and real early traction ('$8K MRR, 24 paying customers, 18% MoM growth (last 4 months)') that demonstrates genuine market demand. The founding team pedigree (ex-Stripe, ex-Notion) is well-matched to the problem domain. These are real strengths that give investors a reason to lean in.

However, the deck is critically incomplete at 6 slides for a seed round. The seed-stage framework expects 12–15 slides, and Acmecorp is missing six slides that investors consider non-negotiable: Competition, Market Sizing, Business Model, GTM, Why Now, and Financials. Each of these missing sections represents a diligence question that will be raised in the first meeting — having no answer ready signals the team hasn't thought through the full business. DocSend data is clear: VCs spend 88% more time on the competition slide in successful decks; its absence alone will trigger skepticism.

The narrative arc has the right bones (Problem → Solution → Traction → Team → Ask) but skips Why Now and proof of defensibility entirely. The 'AI-native' positioning in the title is a liability, not an asset, because it raises expectations (compute economics, retention rebasing, defensibility beyond the API layer) that the current deck does not address anywhere. In 2026's AI-saturated market, an unsubstantiated 'AI-native' claim reads as marketing, not engineering.

The ask slide ('Raising $1.2M seed at $8M post') states terms without milestones, use of funds, or runway — failing the 2026 standard of tying dollars to milestones to next financing. The valuation at ~80x current ARR is aggressive and will face scrutiny without a strong forward trajectory story.

The highest-leverage next step is not polishing the existing slides — it is building the six missing slides, particularly Competition and Business Model, which investors will probe immediately. Once those are in place, the team should revisit the solution slide (add product evidence and before→after workflow) and the ask slide (add milestones and use of funds). A complete seed deck with these additions would be genuinely competitive given the traction signal already present.

## Coaching Commentary

### What's Working — Protect These

**1. The problem is quantified.** "20+ hours/week" is a real number. Most early-stage decks say "developers are frustrated" and stop there. You've put a time cost on the pain, which is the first move toward making it feel urgent. Per YC's "problem before solution" principle, quantified pain dramatically increases investor engagement.

**2. The founding team has legitimate pedigree.** Ex-Stripe (eng) and ex-Notion (product) is a credible pairing for a developer-tooling company. Stripe is one of the most respected engineering cultures in the industry; Notion brings product-led growth intuition. That combination signals you understand both the technical infrastructure and the adoption dynamics. Investors will notice.

**3. The core narrative spine exists.** Problem → Solution → Team → Ask is the fundamental arc, and you have it. Many decks at this stage are a disconnected collection of slides. You have a thread. That's a foundation to build on, not start over from.

---

### Highest-Leverage Change: Add the Five Missing Slides

This is not five separate fixes — it is one structural gap that accounts for the majority of your 18 failures. The deck is currently 6 slides. A seed-stage deck needs 10-12. The missing slides are: **Why Now, Market Sizing, Competition, Business Model, and GTM.** Every one of these is a critical omission at seed.

Here's why each one matters from an investor's seat:

- **Why Now** answers the question every investor is silently asking: "If this problem has existed for years, why will it get solved in the next 18 months?" Per Sequoia's "Why wasn't this built before?" standard, the absence of a why-now slide signals either that you haven't thought about market timing or that the timing isn't actually compelling. Either reading is damaging.

- **Market Sizing** done bottom-up (ICP count × willingness to pay × adoption rate) shows you understand your customers. A top-down TAM number ("$50B market") tells investors nothing — they've seen it a thousand times. A bottom-up calculation shows discipline. This is a non-negotiable for seed per standard VC practice.

- **Competition** is the slide most founders dread and most investors scrutinize hardest. DocSend data shows investors spend 88% more time on competition in funded decks versus unfunded ones. An absent competition slide doesn't signal you have no competitors — it signals you haven't done the work, or you're hiding something. Neither is acceptable. Show the landscape honestly. Your differentiation will be more credible for it.

- **Business Model** needs to answer three questions: Who pays? How much? What are the margins? Without this, "raising $1.2M seed" floats in a vacuum — investors can't model what the business looks like at scale, and they won't ask in a meeting what they couldn't figure out from the deck.

- **GTM** (go-to-market) should show your ICP, the channel, and early proof of that channel working. Developer tools live or die on distribution. Ex-Stripe and ex-Notion should have strong intuitions here — surface them.

Adding these five slides with real content will raise your score substantially and, more importantly, will make the deck fundable.

### The AI Claim Needs Resolution

Your deck uses "AI-native" in the tagline but contains no AI-specific content anywhere. This is your most credibility-damaging issue and it compounds every other weakness.

Investors reading a seed deck in 2026 are acutely attuned to unsubstantiated AI claims. "AI-native" without any of the following — ML in the value prop, inference costs in COGS, foundation model or fine-tuning mention, AI-specific retention metrics — reads as either marketing inflation or confusion about what the product actually does. Per a16z's AI company evaluation framework, an API wrapper without a moat is not defensible, and a claim without proof is worse than no claim at all.

You have two paths: (1) Remove "AI-native" from the positioning until you can substantiate it with specific AI capabilities, compute economics, and defensibility narrative. (2) Add a slide that shows what the AI actually does, what data flywheel or workflow embeddedness creates lock-in, and what your path to 60%+ gross margins looks like as inference costs are real COGS. Path 2 is the right long-term answer. Path 1 is the right move for this fundraise if the AI capabilities aren't production-ready yet.

Slide 6 has the right number ($1.2M seed at $8M post) but stops there. The 2026 fundraising standard requires tying dollars to milestones to next-round readiness. Investors want to know: what does $1.2M buy you, what does "success" look like in 18 months, and what metrics will you need to raise your Series A? Three sentences. Add them.

## Coaching Commentary

### What's Working — Protect These

**1. The problem is quantified.** "20+ hours/week" is a real number. Most early-stage decks say "developers are frustrated" and stop there. You've put a time cost on the pain, which is the first move toward making it feel urgent. Per YC's "problem before solution" principle, quantified pain dramatically increases investor engagement.

**2. The founding team has legitimate pedigree.** Ex-Stripe (eng) and ex-Notion (product) is a credible pairing for a developer-tooling company. Stripe is one of the most respected engineering cultures in the industry; Notion brings product-led growth intuition. That combination signals you understand both the technical infrastructure and the adoption dynamics. Investors will notice.

**3. The core narrative spine exists.** Problem → Solution → Team → Ask is the fundamental arc, and you have it. Many decks at this stage are a disconnected collection of slides. You have a thread. That's a foundation to build on, not start over from.

---

### Highest-Leverage Change: Add the Five Missing Slides

This is not five separate fixes — it is one structural gap that accounts for the majority of your 18 failures. The deck is currently 6 slides. A seed-stage deck needs 10-12. The missing slides are: **Why Now, Market Sizing, Competition, Business Model, and GTM.** Every one of these is a critical omission at seed.

Here's why each one matters from an investor's seat:

- **Why Now** answers the question every investor is silently asking: "If this problem has existed for years, why will it get solved in the next 18 months?" Per Sequoia's "Why wasn't this built before?" standard, the absence of a why-now slide signals either that you haven't thought about market timing or that the timing isn't actually compelling. Either reading is damaging.

- **Market Sizing** done bottom-up (ICP count × willingness to pay × adoption rate) shows you understand your customers. A top-down TAM number ("$50B market") tells investors nothing — they've seen it a thousand times. A bottom-up calculation shows discipline. This is a non-negotiable for seed per standard VC practice.

- **Competition** is the slide most founders dread and most investors scrutinize hardest. DocSend data shows investors spend 88% more time on competition in funded decks versus unfunded ones. An absent competition slide doesn't signal you have no competitors — it signals you haven't done the work, or you're hiding something. Neither is acceptable. Show the landscape honestly. Your differentiation will be more credible for it.

- **Business Model** needs to answer three questions: Who pays? How much? What are the margins? Without this, "raising $1.2M seed" floats in a vacuum — investors can't model what the business looks like at scale, and they won't ask in a meeting what they couldn't figure out from the deck.

- **GTM** (go-to-market) should show your ICP, the channel, and early proof of that channel working. Developer tools live or die on distribution. Ex-Stripe and ex-Notion should have strong intuitions here — surface them.

Adding these five slides with real content will raise your score substantially and, more importantly, will make the deck fundable.

### The AI Claim Needs Resolution

Your deck uses "AI-native" in the tagline but contains no AI-specific content anywhere. This is your most credibility-damaging issue and it compounds every other weakness.

Investors reading a seed deck in 2026 are acutely attuned to unsubstantiated AI claims. "AI-native" without any of the following — ML in the value prop, inference costs in COGS, foundation model or fine-tuning mention, AI-specific retention metrics — reads as either marketing inflation or confusion about what the product actually does. Per a16z's AI company evaluation framework, an API wrapper without a moat is not defensible, and a claim without proof is worse than no claim at all.

You have two paths: (1) Remove "AI-native" from the positioning until you can substantiate it with specific AI capabilities, compute economics, and defensibility narrative. (2) Add a slide that shows what the AI actually does, what data flywheel or workflow embeddedness creates lock-in, and what your path to 60%+ gross margins looks like as inference costs are real COGS. Path 2 is the right long-term answer. Path 1 is the right move for this fundraise if the AI capabilities aren't production-ready yet.

Slide 6 has the right number ($1.2M seed at $8M post) but stops there. The 2026 fundraising standard requires tying dollars to milestones to next-round readiness. Investors want to know: what does $1.2M buy you, what does "success" look like in 18 months, and what metrics will you need to raise your Series A? Three sentences. Add them.

At 21.2% (major revision), the honest answer is: not from a cold read. The deck as it stands signals a very early-stage product with incomplete investor preparation — not necessarily a bad company, but a deck that hasn't finished communicating the opportunity.
